lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Thais Cari de Souza Freitas Ladislau | Lesson 13 -- Asking the Right Question
lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions and polite requests -- could you tell me, do you know if, I was wondering if, would you mind + -ing

listenings.text: Hi Thais, it is Carla from the VP's office, about Thursday. Three quick things. First, could you send me the final numbers for the credit part by Wednesday at noon? I need them for the deck. Second, I was wondering if you could open with the approval rate. The VP wants to understand why approvals fell in May, and whether it is a decision or a problem, so I think that should come first. And third, Mark told me you asked for thirty minutes. That is fine with me, but do you know if thirty is really enough? If it is not, could you let me know today? Then I can move the pricing part to the end. Would you mind calling me back after four? Thanks, Thais.

People often ask me why a direct question can sound rude in English, when the same question in Portuguese or Spanish sounds perfectly normal. The answer is distance. English uses distance to show respect. Could you, would you, I was wondering if: all of these put a little space between you and the request, and that space is what the other person hears as respect. A direct question removes the space. But there is a second mistake, and it is just as common. Some people become so polite that they never actually ask. They say I was wondering, and maybe, and if it is possible, and at the end nobody knows what they wanted. My formula is simple. A polite frame, a clear request, and the reason, in that order. I was wondering if we could have thirty minutes, because the rule needs a clarification. That is polite, and it is not weak.
